channel.title: Plainly Put
channel.description: One topic per episode, anything from bridge engineering to sleep, explained plainly in about twenty-five minutes. Claude researches and writes each episode from a handful of sources, all listed in the show notes, and a synthetic voice reads it. Where the evidence is thin, the episode says so.

item.title: Episode 3: What cold showers actually do
item.description:
Higher-risk topic: cold exposure raises heart rate and blood pressure and can be dangerous with heart conditions, or alone in open water.

A trial of 3,018 adults found that ending a normal shower with 30, 60 or 90 seconds of the coldest tap water for 30 days cut sickness absence from work by 29 percent, but not the number of days people felt ill, and all outcomes were self-reported. The episode explains what cold water does to the body, why the often-quoted dopamine figure comes from an hour in a cold tank rather than a shower, and what reviews say about mood, stress and muscle soreness.

Basic plan: after a normal warm shower, run the coldest water for the last 30 to 60 seconds, three days a week at first. In the main trial, 30, 60 and 90 seconds did not differ. No trial compares ending cold with ending warm. If you have a heart condition, an irregular heartbeat, high blood pressure or take blood pressure medication, ask your doctor first. Avoid cold in the hour or so after strength training if building muscle matters to you. Do not take cold baths or open-water dips alone.

item.title: Episode 2: A short history of Bulgaria
item.description:
Bulgaria was founded around 681, lost to the Byzantine Empire in 1018, refounded in 1185, lost to the Ottomans by the end of the 14th century, and freed in 1878 by a Russian war, though a treaty three months later cut the new state down and set up four unsuccessful wars. The 1876 April Uprising, whose casualty figures are still disputed, and a 1762 history of the Bulgarian people did much to build the sense of nationhood that survived in between.

Key dates: 681, Asparuh's Bulgars secure the right to settle south of the Danube. 864, Orthodox Christianity becomes the state religion. 893, the Council of Preslav moves the capital and makes Old Bulgarian the language of church and state. 927, the Bulgarian Patriarchate is recognised. 1014, Kleidion. 1018, Byzantine conquest. 1185, the uprising of Peter and Asen. 1230, Klokotnitsa. 1385 to 1396, the Ottoman conquest. 1762, Paisiy's history. 1876, the April Uprising. 3 March 1878, San Stefano. 13 July 1878, Berlin. 1885, unification with Eastern Rumelia. 1908, independence. 1946, the republic. 10 November 1989, Zhivkov resigns. 2004, NATO. 2007, the European Union. 2026, the euro.

Where sources disagree: Kleidion's blinded prisoners are given as 15,000 by Skylitzes and 8,000 by the Manasses Chronicle. April Uprising Bulgarian deaths are estimated from about 3,000 to 40,000 depending on the source, and Muslim deaths from 115 to over 1,000. The episode gives the ranges.

Most sources here are reference-work articles that cite historians, and a Library of Congress country study from 1992, so the episode treats details as secondary.

item.title: Episode 1: Serotonin and your gut
item.description:
Higher-risk topic: discusses antidepressants and other prescription drugs, and irritable bowel syndrome.

More than 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, not the brain, and it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Gut serotonin moves food along, signals fullness and nausea to the brainstem, and is carried in platelets, which hold over 95% of the serotonin in the blood and use it in clotting.

In mice, gut bacteria, especially spore-forming species, prompt the gut's own cells to make serotonin: the microbiota accounted for 64% of colonic and 49% of blood serotonin, while bacteria made under 10% directly. These results are in mice and cell models, not yet in people.

The gut talks to the brain along the vagus nerve. A Lactobacillus rhamnosus strain that reduced anxiety-like behaviour in mice, an effect that vanished when the vagus nerve was cut, had no effect over placebo on mood, stress, sleep or cognition in 29 healthy men over 8 weeks.

Drugs acting on gut serotonin have the firmest evidence: 5-HT3 blockers such as ondansetron for chemotherapy nausea, and antidepressants for irritable bowel syndrome. A 2025 meta-analysis of 28 trials (2,475 patients) found tricyclics cut the risk of global symptoms persisting (RR 0.70, moderate certainty), and SSRIs helped abdominal pain (RR 0.74, 7 trials, low certainty). SSRIs can also cause gut side effects, speeding transit or causing constipation. If you take an antidepressant, talk to your prescriber before changing it.
